https://www.politico.eu/article/strait-o.text: Negotiations between Iran and Oman on delineating a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz have reached the final stage, the Iranian Foreign Ministry confirmed on Wednesday. The shipping lane would primarily lie within Iranian territorial waters, with parts extending into Omani waters. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists that “the geographical coordinates of the proposed maritime route have been agreed upon by both sides,” adding that the bilateral process was “professional” and “forward-moving.” Advertisement Advertisement U.S. President Donald Trump announced last weekend that Tehran had asked Washington to hold off any attack on Iran due to the pending agreement on the strait. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . The U.S. reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports on July 14 after hostilities between the two countries resumed. The blockade has since become one of the main sticking points in ceasefire negotiations, with Tehran insisting it must be lifted as part of any broader agreement. The strait remains closed as a result of the military strikes launched by the U.S. and Israel, Baqaei maintained in his remarks.

Plus, how five obscure horses have ended up at the center of a transatlantic betting mystery Martin Belam Mon 17 Aug 2026 07.04 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 07.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Donald Trump has said he is scaling back joint US military drills with South Korea aimed at deterring North Korea, despite military officials from both countries warning that Kim Jong-un’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from the Ukraine war. The president said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”. He added that the drills were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”. Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. Why are there continuing concerns about USS Abraham Lincoln? Democrats have intensified their demands for answers from the Trump administration over conditions onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln amid concern over crew morale, mental health and living conditions. Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator from Arizona, said he blamed the carrier’s prolonged deployment on the unresolved war that Donald Trump started in February with Iran as well as lackluster leadership in general from the Republican president’s administration. Jared Kushner meets Hamas leader before talks with Netanyahu on Gaza View image in fullscreen Jared Kushner is due to meet the Israeli PM. Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPA Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, Jared Kushner, held a rare meeting with Hamas’s political chief on Sunday in Egypt, in a new diplomatic effort to make progress on the stalled Gaza ceasefire. On Monday, Kushner will meet Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who is under pressure after rejecting the new 15-point, US-backed roadmap. The roadmap involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. Israel has killed more than 1,200 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded more than 4,100 since agreeing to the ceasefire on 10 October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Blanche also claimed Trump would never ask him to do something that crossed an ethical or legal line. Blanche added: “I swore to the constitution of the United States, like every cabinet secretary has done, and like every attorney general before me has done. Asked about Trump’s comment that “nothing bad can happen” from advising parents to get six separate shots for their children instead of two, Cassidy told CNN on Sunday: “If it wasn’t so potentially tragic, you would break out laughing at a comment like that.” In other news … View image in fullscreen Hayden Panettiere. Her father, Skip Panettiere, asked for privacy “as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss”. The left-hander was 31 years old when he tore the ulnar collateral ligament in his pitching elbow and had it replaced with a tendon from his right forearm. Arday was pronounced dead on Friday, weeks after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education, following widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements. Bryan Armen Graham looks at what could be a sensational stroke of luck … or something more sinister. Composite: Guardian Design South Korea Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers Raphael Rashid in Seoul Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.50 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Fuel is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv. Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east. Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals. “It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine .” British armed forces intercept Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in Channel Read more Seoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans. But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties. While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles. The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret. It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show. The largest carrier, the sanctioned Layla , made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan. Korea-Russia map Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria , which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok. Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border Read more The third sanctioned tanker, the Chongchon , never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I, at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination. The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment. Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”. According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions , and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner, Eduard Khudainatov , and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions. In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India. Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey. A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade. In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver. On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027. When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.” It said it had expanded its export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them. The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said. The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul. A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.” Explore more on these topics South Korea Russia Ukraine Asia Pacific Oil Commodities news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://business-review.eu/news/muresan-.text: Mureșan government rejected by Parliament, opening constitutional path to unprecedented snap elections The government proposed by prime minister-designate Siegfried Mureșan failed to win Parliament’s confidence on Wednesday, deepening Romania’s nearly five-month political crisis and, for the first time in the current standoff, fulfilling the constitutional conditions that allow President Nicușor Dan to dissolve Parliament and trigger snap elections. The proposed cabinet received 182 votes in favour and 15 against, well short of the 233 votes required for investiture. Mureșan had entered the vote with the backing of PNL, USR, and UDMR, which together control around 170 seats, while both PSD and AUR had announced they would not support the government. The result follows the rejection of Adrian Veștea’s proposed government on June 22, when his cabinet received 189 votes in favour. More than 60 days have now passed since that first failed request for investiture. Under Article 89 of the Romanian Constitution, the president may dissolve Parliament if lawmakers have failed to grant confidence to a government within 60 days of the first request for investiture and after at least two such requests have been rejected. The provision gives the president the option, rather than an obligation, to dissolve Parliament, following consultations with the speakers of the two chambers and parliamentary group leaders. For the first time since the fall of communism, those minimum constitutional conditions have now been met. Previous attempts to reach an early election stopped short of that threshold. In 2009, Lucian Croitoru’s proposed cabinet was rejected, but the subsequently designated Liviu Negoiță never submitted his government to an investiture vote. In 2020, President Klaus Iohannis and the PNL openly pursued early elections after the fall of the Orban government, but the process ended before two investiture requests had been rejected and the full constitutional conditions were met. Read more about Luca Niculescu nominated by Nicușor Dan as a candidate for the post of Prime Minister read more Romania has consequently never held a snap parliamentary election in its post-1989 history. If Nicușor Dan were to use the constitutional mechanism now available to him, it would be the first dissolution of Parliament under Article 89. President has argued against snap elections President Nicușor Dan has so far given little indication that he intends to immediately exercise that option. Speaking on Tuesday, a day before the Mureșan vote, Dan said that snap elections were “not a solution” to the current crisis and would prolong uncertainty. “Snap elections are not a solution. On the contrary, they would continue the instability and lack of confidence among both Romanian citizens and the financial markets,” the president said. He called on parties to look beyond their immediate political interests and bring the government crisis to an end. The Constitutional Court has previously interpreted the dissolution mechanism as an exceptional, last-resort instrument designed to resolve a genuine institutional deadlock. Its 2020 jurisprudence also makes clear that the Constitution does not prevent a president from making further prime ministerial nominations even after the minimum threshold of two failed investiture attempts has been reached. This leaves Dan with significant room for manoeuvre. He can begin the procedure that could lead to Parliament’s dissolution, or resume consultations and attempt to find a candidate capable of securing 233 votes. Attention turns to PSD and AUR Political negotiations are now expected to focus increasingly on PSD, Parliament’s largest party, which has repeatedly said it wants to return to government and has put forward its president, Sorin Grindeanu, for prime minister. Grindeanu said last week that, if nominated, he would speak to all parliamentary parties in an attempt to form what he described as a stable and transparent majority. PSD MEP Victor Negrescu said on Wednesday morning that the party wanted the next governing majority to be built around PSD, while raising the possibility that UDMR could reconsider its current alignment. A Grindeanu nomination has therefore become one of the most frequently discussed scenarios following Mureșan’s expected defeat, although the presidency has made no such announcement. Political speculation around that option has circulated since before Mureșan’s nomination, while PSD has consistently maintained Grindeanu as its candidate. Another increasingly scrutinised scenario is some form of cooperation between PSD and AUR. The two parties jointly brought down Ilie Bolojan’s government in May and their combined parliamentary strength gives them substantial leverage over any new majority. However, there is currently no announced PSD-AUR governing agreement, and together the two parties still fall short of the 233 votes required to install a cabinet. AUR leader George Simion said this week that his party had appointed a negotiating team to hold talks with all political parties on forming a new government. PSD has previously left open the possibility of cooperation with AUR, although Grindeanu has also spoken publicly about the need for a future majority to be based on European values. UDMR parliamentary leader Csoma Botond has meanwhile suggested that Dan could make two further nominations rather than dissolve Parliament immediately, potentially beginning with a political candidate before returning to a technocratic option. Political crisis reaches rating review The renewed uncertainty comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Romania’s public finances. S&P Global Ratings is scheduled to review Romania’s sovereign rating on October 2, just two days after Wednesday’s failed investiture vote. The prolonged government crisis has increased scrutiny of Romania’s investment-grade status, with rating agencies closely watching political stability and the credibility of fiscal consolidation. S&P currently rates Romania at BBB-, the lowest investment-grade level, with a negative outlook. In its April assessment, the agency said a downgrade could follow if Romania deviated significantly from its fiscal consolidation path, while identifying implementation risks, political tensions, and delays to EU funding as important vulnerabilities. The political crisis has also become entangled in a separate controversy involving Grindeanu and US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle. The Wall Street Journal, the Financial Times and Romanian media reported this week on remarks allegedly made by Guilfoyle at a March dinner in Athens suggesting that Washington could influence changes of government in the region. Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the account. The reports drew fresh attention to a March 31 meeting between Guilfoyle and Grindeanu in Bucharest, held several weeks before PSD joined the vote that brought down Bolojan’s government. Grindeanu has rejected suggestions that the meeting was connected either to Bolojan’s removal or to commercial negotiations involving US gas supplies. He said he had not discussed gas contracts with Guilfoyle and described allegations of US involvement in the government’s fall as false. With the Mureșan option now defeated, the immediate decision returns to Cotroceni. Dan must choose between testing Parliament with another nominee and beginning a constitutional process that could ultimately produce Romania’s first snap parliamentary election since 1989. https://hungarytoday.hu/back-to-reality-.text: Back to Reality: IMF Sends Hungary a Crippling Austerity Wishlist An International Monetary Fund (IMF) delegation visited Hungary during the last week of September and the first week of October to hold consultations with Hungarian authorities. At the conclusion of the visit, the IMF issued a detailed statement, the contents of which were reported by Világgazdaság . One of FIDESZ’s main electoral promises before the 2010 elections was “sending the IMF” packing, as they put it. After their historic win, the Orbán government has managed to repay their multi billion euro loan early in August 2013. In Viktor Orbán’s own interpretation, the crippling austerity measures that the IMF has imposed on the Hungarian population was not only a social issue, it was a matter of national sovereignty. After the April elections, it did not take long for the IMF to return to Hungary with the advent of a new, pro-EU government. Even though Brussels has promised the release of billions of European funds to the Magyar government for the alleged progress they made in restoring the rule-of-law in Hungary, there have been reports of a bridging loan from the IMF to fill the gap until the money from Brussels arrives. In a statement, IMF experts who visited Hungary in September and October have noted that the economy is being held back by several factors simultaneously: weak investment appetite, a widening gap between wages and productivity, a challenging global environment, and an aging population. Meanwhile, despite pre-election promises to the opposite, this year’s budget deficit is projected to range between 7% and 7.5% of GDP, and public debt is on the rise. Given these challenges, the IMF is urging the implementation of a reform package. The Fund has put forward several proposals for a potential TISZA government. Péter Magyar casting his ballot during the election after campaigning on cheaper energy prices, stronger social net, better pensions. Photo: MTI /Hegedüs Róbert 1. Multi-rate personal income tax and corporate tax hike According to the international organization, the Hungarian tax system is the least progressive in the OECD and generates less tax revenue than necessary, while the flat personal income tax and corporate tax rates are among the lowest in the region. The IMF suggests that a multi-rate tax system and the restructuring of tax allowances would boost both revenue and labor market activity. Additionally, raising the corporate tax rate was proposed, as was the idea that sector-specific special taxes could eventually be phased out. 2. Fewer VAT exemptions and tax allowances The Fund advocates for narrowing certain exemptions and preferential rates while urging support for households in need. This concept is familiar: it is known as the means-testing principle. 3. Phasing out utility cost reductions Scaling back subsidized energy consumption thresholds—essentially the utility cost reduction scheme—is also on the list. As noted, phasing out “distorted” price caps and energy subsidies will be challenging, but it is a necessary step. 4. Phasing out the “Home-start” program According to the IMF, remaining loan subsidy programs for first-time property buyers should be phased out, as they distort credit allocation and undermine the effectiveness of monetary policy. 5. Raising the retirement age With pension and healthcare expenditures projected to rise by nearly four percentage points of GDP by 2050, the Fund proposes linking the retirement age to life expectancy—which effectively means raising the retirement age. Additionally, the IMF advocates for the gradual elimination of early retirement options and a recalculation of pension benefits. Pensioners. Photo: Pixabay 6. Privatization? Finally, the report alluded to the potential sale of state-owned enterprises that the Orbán governments had previously repurchased from foreign owners. It noted that state-owned companies tend to be consistently less profitable and less productive than private firms operating in the same sectors. Furthermore, a significant state presence crowds out private enterprises and can weaken the performance of private-sector competitors. Regarding the Monetary Fund’s recommendations, we should also cite the latest country report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). The document proposes reforming the pension system and raising the retirement age; furthermore, it suggests—among other measures—making personal income tax more progressive, reviewing tax allowances, and not least, phasing out the utility price reduction scheme. In other words, should the TISZA government take the IMF’s guidance as is widely expected to happen, it will effectively phase out all the measures of the previous Orbán government that were meant to return national assets into the hands of the State or to Hungarian enterprise, end energy price caps that have made household energy and heating bills the lowest in the EU, shut down favorable loans for first-time property buyers, and implement austerity measures that have impoverished millions of Hungarian citizens during the previous socialist governments of Ferenc Gyurcsány and Gordon Bajnai (2004-2010). Should the Magyar government take the IMF’s advice, raising the pensions age would also introduce a deeply unpopular measure that has not been hinted at by the winners during the 2026 election campaign. Analysts expect inflation to rise gradually after its summer low.
